title: A Chief of Staff 30-60-90 Day Plan (With Template)
summary: A chief of staff 30-60-90 day plan: what to learn, fix and own in your first three months, common mistakes, and a template to share with your CEO.
body_markdown:
A chief of staff 30-60-90 day plan answers the question every new chief of staff and their CEO are quietly asking: what does success look like, and how fast? The role is famously hard to define. It changes from company to company, and sometimes from month to month. A clear plan for your first 90 days is how you turn that ambiguity into trust.


The good news is that strong first quarters follow a pattern. **Learn before you act, fix one thing well, then take ownership of something visible.**


Here's a plan you can adapt, the mistakes to avoid, and a template to share with your CEO in week one.


## Key takeaways


-


**Days 1 to 30: listen and map.** Meet every leader, audit the operating rhythm and write a short diagnosis. Change very little.


-


**Days 31 to 60: fix one thing.** Usually the weekly leadership meeting or the way commitments are tracked.


-


**Days 61 to 90: own something.** A metric, a cross-functional initiative or the operating rhythm itself, with a written scope agreed with your CEO.


## Before day one: agree on what success means


The most important conversation happens before you start, or in your first week. Sit down with your CEO and agree on:


-


**Why this role exists now.** What's breaking, or what does the CEO want off their plate?


-


**Your scope.** Which areas are yours, which are shared and which are off limits?


-


**How you'll work together.** A weekly sync, how urgent requests reach you and expectations about evenings and weekends.


-


**What a great first 90 days looks like** in the CEO's own words.


Write it down and share it back. It becomes the first version of your 30-60-90 day plan. If you're still clarifying the role itself, our guide to what a chief of staff actually does is a useful starting point for that conversation.


## Days 1 to 30: listen, map and diagnose


Your first month is mostly invisible, and that's the point. You're building context and trust.


**Meet every leader one-on-one in the first two weeks.** Ask each of them the same questions, so you can compare answers:


1.


What are the company's top priorities right now?


2.


What's working well that we should protect?


3.


What's the biggest thing slowing your team down?


4.


Where do decisions get stuck?


5.


How can I be most useful to you?


**Audit the operating rhythm.** List every recurring leadership meeting. For each one, note its purpose, who attends and what decisions it actually produced last month. Many will have produced none.


**Trace a few recent decisions.** Pick two or three significant decisions from the last quarter and map how they really got made: who was involved, how long it took and whether they stuck.


**Shadow the CEO.** Sit in on as many meetings as you can. Notice what they spend time on that someone else could handle.


**Day 30 deliverable:** a one-page diagnosis for your CEO with what you heard, the three biggest problems you see, and supporting evidence. Hold off on solutions for now. Showing that you understand the problem buys you the credibility to fix it.


## Days 31 to 60: fix one thing well


Now you act, but narrowly. One visible, well-executed fix earns more trust than five half-finished ones.


**Pick the fix with the widest impact.** For most new chiefs of staff, it's one of these:


-


**The weekly leadership meeting.** Introduce written pre-reads, agendas written as decisions, a decision log and a hard stop.


-


**Commitment tracking.** Make sure every action item from leadership meetings has an owner and a date, and is tracked somewhere everyone can see. Our guide on how to keep track of follow-ups at work covers the habits.


-


**Priority clarity.** If leaders named different top priorities in your one-on-ones, run a session to agree on the top three for the quarter.


**Propose the operating rhythm you want to build.** Show the current state, the proposed state, which meetings to cut and roughly how many hours it saves. (Our chief of staff operating rhythm guide includes a one-page template.)


**Set up your own system.** By now you're tracking dozens of threads. Choose the tools you'll run the job on. See our guide to the best tools for chiefs of staff.


**Day 60 deliverable:** one fix shipped and working, plus a proposal for the operating rhythm.


## Days 61 to 90: own something visible


By the end of your first quarter, you should own something the company can see.


**Take ownership of a cross-functional outcome.** That could be:


-


A metric that crosses teams, like hiring velocity, forecast accuracy or on-time launches, reported weekly


-


A strategic initiative the CEO has wanted to start but hasn't had capacity for


-


The operating rhythm itself, now rolled out across the leadership team


**Run your first quarterly planning cycle** , or at least support it, so the company's priorities for next quarter are clear and owned.


**Day 90 deliverable:** a 30-minute review with your CEO covering what you found, what you fixed, what you now own and your priorities for the next quarter. End it by agreeing in writing on your scope for the next six months.


## Common mistakes in a chief of staff's first 90 days


-


**Fixing everything in month one.** You'll fix the wrong things and spend credibility you haven't earned yet.


-


**Only hearing the loudest voices.** Make sure quieter leaders get as much of your time as the vocal ones.


-


**Taking sides too early.** Your value is being trusted by everyone on the leadership team. Stay neutral until you understand the history.


-


**Becoming a dumping ground.** If you take every task the CEO forwards, you'll be too busy to do the job. Agree on what's yours early.


-


**No written scope.** Without a written agreement, the role drifts, and so does how you're evaluated.


-


**Tracking everything in your head.** It works for a few weeks, then something important slips. Build your system early.

Copy this into a doc and share it with your CEO in week one.

## FAQ


**What should a chief of staff do in the first 30 days?**


Listen and map. Meet every leader one-on-one, audit the recurring leadership meetings, trace how recent decisions were made, shadow the CEO and finish the month with a one-page diagnosis.


**What should be in a chief of staff 30-60-90 day plan?**


Clear goals for each phase (learn, fix, own), key activities, a deliverable at days 30, 60 and 90, how the CEO will know it's working and scheduled check-ins. Agree on it with your CEO in your first week.


**How do you succeed as a new chief of staff?**


Earn trust before making big changes, fix one visible problem well, take ownership of a clear outcome by day 90 and agree on your scope in writing. Building a reliable system for tracking commitments early makes all of this easier.


**What is the biggest mistake new chiefs of staff make?**


Trying to fix everything in the first month. It spends credibility you haven't earned yet and often fixes the wrong problems.


**Should a chief of staff own a metric?**


Usually, yes, by around day 90. Owning a visible cross-functional metric or initiative makes your impact clear and keeps the role from becoming purely reactive.


**How is a chief of staff different from an executive assistant?**


A chief of staff extends the CEO's judgment across the company, while an executive assistant manages their calendar, inbox and logistics. See our guide to[chief of staff vs. executive assistant.](https://www.bondapp.io/insights/chief-of-staff-vs-executive-assistant)
